M8.Perceptron.Title: Neurons as classifiers: perceptron and backpropagation
M8.Perceptron.Lead: In supervised learning every training example comes with the desired answer. The system has to learn parameters that also give correct answers for new, unseen inputs – a discrete class label (classification) or a continuous value (regression). Neural networks approach both with neuron-like units that weight and sum their inputs.
M8.Perceptron.C1.Title: Classification is geometry
M8.Perceptron.C1.Text: An input u = (u₁, …, u_n) is a point in an n-dimensional feature space. To separate two classes we look for a decision surface with one class on each side; the simplest is a hyperplane wᵀu − μ = 0 (a line in 2-D). The weight vector w is perpendicular to it and μ shifts it. Learning means setting the orientation and position of this surface.
M8.Perceptron.C2.Title: The perceptron and its learning rule
M8.Perceptron.C2.Text: The perceptron simplifies a neuron radically: weighted sum, then a hard threshold, v = Θ(wᵀu − μ) = ±1. For each example with desired output v^d: Δw = ε(v^d − v)u and Δμ = −ε(v^d − v). Correctly classified examples cause no change; a mistake pushes the line so that the example moves to the right side. For linearly separable data the perceptron convergence theorem guarantees a separating line after finitely many updates. The perceptron does not memorize points – it learns a direction from its mistakes.
M8.Perceptron.C3.Title: The limit: XOR
M8.Perceptron.C3.Text: One perceptron can only solve problems that a single hyperplane separates. XOR violates this: the positive examples sit in two opposite corners, the negative ones in the other two – no line separates them. The solution is a hidden layer: several units draw several lines, and their combination yields a nonlinear decision boundary. This is the multilayer perceptron (MLP), the ancestor of deep networks.
M8.Perceptron.C4.Title: Sigmoid units and backpropagation
M8.Perceptron.C4.Text: The hard threshold has no useful derivative. A sigmoid g(a) = 1/(1 + e^(−βa)) is smooth (large β approaches the hard threshold), so the error E = ½Σ(d − v)² can be minimized by gradient descent. Backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute how much every weight contributed to the output error. It is not a physical “error signal sent back”, but the computation of partial derivatives. The same idea, with ReLUs, cross-entropy and better optimizers, drives deep learning today; the course's truck-backing example even learns a steering control function.
M8.Perceptron.Formulas:
wᵀu − μ = 0 | The decision hyperplane; w is perpendicular to it.
v = Θ(wᵀu − μ),   Θ(x) = +1 if x > 0, else −1 | The perceptron.
Δw_i = ε (v^d − v) u_i,    Δμ = −ε (v^d − v) | Perceptron learning rule – no change for correct answers.
g(a) = 1 / (1 + exp(−β a)) | Sigmoid activation; β sets the steepness.
E = ½ Σ_i (d_i − v_i)²,   Δw = −ε ∂E/∂w | Squared error minimized by gradient descent / backpropagation.
M8.Perceptron.Bio: A real neuron integrates thousands of synaptic inputs on its dendrites and fires when the membrane reaches threshold – the perceptron keeps only the weighted sum and the threshold. Cerebellar Purkinje cells, with their climbing-fibre “teacher” signal, are a classic biological candidate for perceptron-like supervised learning.
M8.Perceptron.ML: The perceptron is the simplest linear classifier; logistic regression is its sigmoid version. Adding hidden layers and training with backpropagation gives the multilayer perceptron – the basis of deep learning, which today uses ReLU activations, cross-entropy loss, normalization and adaptive optimizers.
M8.Perceptron.Takeaways:
A perceptron is a linear classifier: a weighted sum and a threshold define a hyperplane.
The perceptron rule changes weights only after mistakes and converges for linearly separable data.
XOR is not linearly separable – a hidden layer is needed.
Sigmoid units make the network differentiable; backpropagation computes the gradients with the chain rule.
M8.Perceptron.Q1: Why is the perceptron a linear classifier?
M8.Perceptron.A1: Because its decision depends only on which side of the hyperplane wᵀu − μ = 0 the input lies.
M8.Perceptron.Q2: Why can't a single perceptron solve XOR?
M8.Perceptron.A2: The two XOR classes cannot be separated by a single line/hyperplane; a nonlinear representation or a hidden layer is needed.
M8.Perceptron.Q3: What is the difference between classification and regression?
M8.Perceptron.A3: Classification predicts a discrete class label, regression a continuous quantity.
M8.Perceptron.A4: The partial derivatives of the output error with respect to every weight, layer by layer, using the chain rule – then gradient descent updates the weights.
M8.Perceptron.Guide:
With “Separable” data press Train: every mistake (yellow ring) tilts the line until all points are correct.
Try AND and OR: both are linearly separable.
Try XOR with the single perceptron – it never settles. Switch to the multilayer network and train.
The faint dashed lines of the MLP are its hidden units: their combination bends the boundary.
Left-click adds a + example, right-click a − example – build your own puzzle.
M8.Perceptron.SimpleTitle: In plain words: drawing one straight line between two groups
M8.Perceptron.Simple: Imagine blue and pink marbles on a table and a ruler you may place anywhere. The perceptron tries to put the ruler between the colours: whenever a marble is on the wrong side, it nudges the ruler a little. If the colours can be separated by a straight line, it will find one. But if blue marbles sit in two opposite corners and pink ones in the other two (XOR), no single ruler can do it – you need several rulers combined, which is exactly what a network with a hidden layer does.
M8.Perceptron.Data.Tip: Two-class problems in the plane. Teal circles: class +1, pink squares: class −1.
M8.Perceptron.ClickHint: Left-click: add a +1 example. Right-click: add a −1 example.
M8.Perceptron.Model.Tip: Single perceptron (linear, hard threshold) or a two-layer network of sigmoid units trained with backpropagation.
M8.Perceptron.Hidden.Tip: Number of sigmoid units in the hidden layer. XOR needs at least 2.
M8.Perceptron.Beta.Tip: Steepness of the sigmoid: large β approaches the hard threshold of the perceptron.
M8.Perceptron.Plane.Tip: Background: the model's decision (teal = +1, pink = −1; for the MLP shading = confidence). Yellow line and arrow: perceptron boundary and its weight vector w. Red rings: misclassified examples. Big ring: last presented example (yellow = caused an update).
M8.Perceptron.Curve.Tip: Perceptron: accuracy after every presentation. MLP: mean squared error after every epoch.
M8.Perceptron.Explain.Learning: Every misclassified example tilts or shifts the line by ε(v^d − v)u. Correct examples leave it unchanged.
M8.Perceptron.Explain.Done: All examples are on the correct side – no more mistakes, so learning stops. A separating hyperplane has been found.
M8.Perceptron.Explain.Hard: This problem is not linearly separable: whatever line the perceptron chooses, some examples stay wrong, so the weights keep jumping. Switch to the multilayer network.
M8.Perceptron.Explain.Mlp: The MLP minimizes the squared error by gradient descent; the shading shows its graded output g(·) between the classes.
M8.Perceptron.Explain.MlpHard: Each hidden unit draws one line (dashed); the output unit combines their half-planes into a curved boundary – that is how a hidden layer solves XOR-like problems.
M8.Td.Title: Reinforcement learning: predicting rewards
M8.Td.Lead: In reinforcement learning there is no “correct answer” for each state. The agent acts, the environment answers with rewards, and the system must learn from experience which states and events promise later reward. The key tool is the temporal-difference (TD) prediction error – which turns out to look remarkably like the firing of dopamine neurons.
M8.Td.C1.Title: Rewards come late
M8.Td.C1.Text: A reward often arrives later than the stimulus or decision that predicted it – the temporal credit-assignment problem. In Pavlov's experiment a bell, repeatedly followed by food, becomes a predictor of food. The value of a state is the expected sum of future rewards from it: v(t) ≈ E[Σ_τ r(t + τ)] (often discounted by γ^τ).
M8.Td.C2.Title: Bootstrapping: the TD error
M8.Td.C2.Text: The total future reward is not known yet at time t. TD learning replaces it by the immediate reward plus the next value estimate: δ(t) = r(t) + v(t+1) − v(t). δ > 0: things went better than expected; δ < 0: worse; δ ≈ 0: as predicted. Because one estimate is trained by another, there is no need to wait for the end of the trial.
M8.Td.C3.Title: The prediction moves back in time
M8.Td.C3.Text: With a tapped-delay-line stimulus representation, v(t) = Σ_τ w(τ) u(t − τ) and Δw(τ) = ε δ(t) u(t − τ). Early in learning only the unexpected reward produces an error. Over trials the positive error moves backwards, until the predictive stimulus itself becomes the surprising event and the fully expected reward no longer produces any error.
M8.Td.C4.Title: Dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error
M8.Td.C4.Text: Dopaminergic neurons of the VTA show exactly this pattern (Schultz, Dayan & Montague 1997): a burst to an unexpected reward; after learning, a burst to the cue and none to the predicted reward; and if a predicted reward is omitted, a dip below baseline at the expected time – a negative prediction error. Dopamine does more than carry one scalar RL signal (motivation, movement, salience), but the RPE model is remarkably successful.
M8.Td.Formulas:
v(t) ≈ E[ Σ_(τ=0…T−t) r(t + τ) ] | Value: expected sum of future rewards.
δ(t) = r(t) + v(t + 1) − v(t) | Temporal-difference (reward prediction) error.
v(t) = Σ_τ w(τ) u(t − τ) | Prediction from a delay-line representation of the cue.
Δw(τ) = ε · δ(t) · u(t − τ) | TD learning rule.
M8.Td.Bio: The midbrain dopamine system (VTA, substantia nigra) projects widely to striatum and cortex. Its phasic bursts and dips follow the reward prediction error in many experiments; the dopamine signal is thought to gate plasticity at cortico-striatal synapses.
M8.Td.ML: TD learning is the core of modern value-based RL (TD(λ), Q-learning, deep Q-networks). Discounting by γ makes infinite sums converge and expresses a preference for earlier rewards.
M8.Td.Takeaways:
The value of a state is the expected sum of future rewards, not the immediate reward.
The TD error δ = r + v(t+1) − v(t) is not simply the reward: it compares reward and two successive estimates.
Over learning the error moves from the reward back to the predicting cue.
Dopamine neurons show this pattern, including the dip when an expected reward is omitted.
M8.Td.Q1: What does the TD error δ(t) represent?
M8.Td.A1: Based on the reward and two successive value estimates, how much better or worse the outcome was than expected.
M8.Td.Q2: Why is TD learning advantageous for online learning compared with using the full return?
M8.Td.A2: It does not need to wait for the end of the episode; it bootstraps from the next value estimate.
M8.Td.Q3: What happens to dopamine firing when an expected reward is omitted?
M8.Td.A3: It drops below baseline at the time the reward was expected – a negative prediction error.
M8.Td.Q4: Why does the dopamine response move from the reward to the cue during learning?
M8.Td.A4: Once the cue predicts the reward, the reward is no longer surprising (δ ≈ 0 there), while the cue's unexpected appearance raises the predicted value – so the positive error appears at the cue.
M8.Td.Guide:
Press “Auto run” and watch the heatmap: the bright teal error stripe moves from the reward time to the cue.
After learning, press “Omit reward”: a blue dip appears exactly when the reward was expected.
Press “Reward without cue”: an unexpected reward gives a burst again.
Lower the reward probability to 0.5: errors appear at both cue and reward (uncertainty).
Move the reward time and watch the error travel back again.
M8.Td.SimpleTitle: In plain words: the brain's “better than expected” signal
M8.Td.Simple: Think of a dog hearing a bell before dinner. The first time, dinner is a pleasant surprise – a burst of “better than expected!”. After many evenings the bell itself becomes the good news, and dinner is merely what was promised: no surprise, no burst. But if one evening the bell rings and no food comes, there is a clear “worse than expected!” dip. Dopamine neurons in our brain send exactly this kind of signal, and the TD formula describes it.
M8.Td.Protocol.Tip: Each trial: a cue at t = 15, a reward later. The TD learner updates its predictions after every trial.
M8.Td.Omission.Tip: Cue as usual, but the expected reward is withheld.
M8.Td.RewardTime.Tip: Time step of the reward (the cue is at t = 15).
M8.Td.Probability.Tip: Partial reinforcement: below 1 the reward sometimes fails to come.
M8.Td.Epsilon.Tip: Learning rate of the TD rule.
M8.Td.Gamma.Tip: Discount factor; 1 = the course's undiscounted sum.
M8.Td.Heatmap.Tip: Rows: the last 60 trials (newest at the bottom); columns: time within the trial. Teal/positive and pink/negative errors.
M8.Td.LastTrial.Tip: Top: the learned value prediction v(t). Bottom: model dopamine neuron, 5 Hz baseline + 25 Hz per unit of δ(t).
M8.Td.Readout: trial {0}   δ at cue = {1}   δ at reward = {2}   v after cue = {3}
M8.Td.Explain.Early: Early trials: nothing predicts the reward yet, so it is a pure surprise – a large positive error at the reward time.
M8.Td.Explain.Learning: Learning: the prediction is growing backwards from the reward towards the cue; part of the surprise is still at the reward.
M8.Td.Explain.Learned: Learned: the cue now carries the surprise (burst at the cue), while the fully predicted reward produces no error.
M8.Td.Explain.Omission: Omission: the prediction expected a reward that did not come – δ < 0 at that moment, the dopamine neuron pauses below baseline.
M8.Td.Explain.RewardOnly: Unexpected reward: without the cue nothing was predicted, so the reward is surprising again – a positive burst.
M8.Td.Shift: The error moves to the cue
M8.Td.Shift.Tip: TD error at the cue and at the reward time in every trial – the two classic dopamine peaks.
M8.ActorCritic.Title: Reinforcement learning: action selection and actor–critic
M8.ActorCritic.Lead: Predicting rewards is not enough – the agent also has to choose actions. The mapping from states to actions is the policy π(a|s); the goal is a policy that maximizes the expected future reward. The actor–critic architecture splits the job: a critic evaluates, an actor decides, and both learn from the same TD error.
M8.ActorCritic.C1.Title: State, action, policy, value
M8.ActorCritic.C1.Text: In the course's “rat in a barn” example the states are locations (A, B, C), the actions left or right turns, and the end branches give different rewards. For a fixed policy, the value v(s) is the expected future reward when starting from state s.
M8.ActorCritic.C2.Title: Policy evaluation with TD
M8.ActorCritic.C2.Text: Under the random policy every action is equally likely, so the value of B and C is the average of their rewards and the value of A the average of B and C. The same values can be learned from experience: V(s) ← V(s) + α[r + V(s′) − V(s)]. The update is local and online – it needs only the current state, the reward and the next state's estimate.
M8.ActorCritic.C3.Title: Exploration vs exploitation
M8.ActorCritic.C3.Text: Always choosing the action that looks best now (greedy) can trap the agent in a poor strategy; exploration tries new options, exploitation uses known good ones. A softmax policy gives higher-valued actions higher probability but keeps the others possible: π(a|s) ∝ exp(βQ(s,a)). Small β is nearly random, large β nearly greedy.
M8.ActorCritic.C4.Title: Actor and critic
M8.ActorCritic.C4.Text: The critic estimates state values and evaluates each experience with the TD error. The actor holds the policy (action preferences m(s,a)) and changes it so that actions followed by positive δ become more likely and those followed by negative δ less likely. Modern policy-gradient and actor–critic algorithms are refined versions of this logic. Functionally, the cortex may provide the state, striatal loops the actor and critic, and dopamine the TD-like teaching signal – an analogy, not a one-to-one mapping.
M8.ActorCritic.Formulas:
V(s) ← V(s) + α [ r + V(s′) − V(s) ] | Critic: TD value learning (policy evaluation).
δ = r + V(s′) − V(s) | The shared teaching signal.
π(a|s) = exp(β m(s,a)) / Σ_b exp(β m(s,b)) | Softmax policy with inverse temperature β.
m(s,a′) ← m(s,a′) + ε (δ_aa′ − π(a′|s)) δ | Actor: the chosen action a becomes more likely after positive δ.
M8.ActorCritic.Bio: Actor–critic models are often compared with the basal ganglia: dorsal striatum as actor (action selection), ventral striatum as critic (value), dopamine as the TD error. This is a functional analogy that has inspired many experiments, not an exact anatomical mapping.
M8.ActorCritic.ML: Policy-gradient methods (REINFORCE, A2C/A3C, PPO) optimize a differentiable policy; the critic reduces the variance of the gradient estimate. Value-based selection relates to dynamic programming and the Bellman optimality equations in Markov environments.
M8.ActorCritic.Takeaways:
The policy says which action to choose in which state; value is the expected future reward.
TD learning evaluates a policy online from experience.
Softmax with β balances exploration and exploitation.
Actor–critic: the critic evaluates (TD error), the actor improves the policy with the same signal.
M8.ActorCritic.Q1: What is the job of the critic and of the actor?
M8.ActorCritic.A1: The critic estimates value and provides the TD error; the actor represents and improves the policy.
M8.ActorCritic.Q2: What does the exploration–exploitation dilemma mean?
M8.ActorCritic.A2: The trade-off between trying new options and using the action currently known to be best.
M8.ActorCritic.Q3: What are the state values under the random policy in the barn (rewards 0/5 and 2/0)?
M8.ActorCritic.Q4: How does β change the softmax policy?
M8.ActorCritic.A4: Small β makes the choices nearly random (exploration), large β nearly greedy (exploitation).
M8.ActorCritic.Guide:
Choose “Policy evaluation” and run: V(A), V(B), V(C) approach the dotted random-policy values 1.75, 2.5, 1.
Switch to “Actor–Critic”: the branches to B and to the 5-reward thicken – the rat learns the best route.
Watch the δ flashes: green when a move went better than expected, red when worse.
Set β to 0 (random) or 5 (greedy) and compare how fast and how well it learns.
Move the food: put the big reward at C → L and see the policy re-learn.
M8.ActorCritic.SimpleTitle: In plain words: a rat, a map and a coach
M8.ActorCritic.Simple: A rat enters a barn and must turn left or right twice to reach some food. It has two helpers in its head. The coach (critic) keeps notes on how good every junction is and shouts “better than I thought!” or “worse than I thought!” after each move. The player (actor) decides where to turn and simply listens to the coach: moves that earned a “better!” are repeated more often. After some runs the rat goes straight to the biggest pile of food.
M8.ActorCritic.Mode.Tip: Policy evaluation: only the critic learns, the rat turns randomly. Actor–Critic: the policy learns too.
M8.ActorCritic.Beta.Tip: Inverse temperature of the softmax: 0 = random choices, large = almost always the preferred action.
M8.ActorCritic.Food.Tip: Rewards of the four end branches (course values: B→L 0, B→R 5, C→L 2, C→R 0).
M8.ActorCritic.Barn.Tip: Node brightness: state value V(s). Branch width: probability of taking it. Rings: TD error of the last run (green +, red −). The rat replays its last run.
M8.ActorCritic.Explain.Evaluation: Policy evaluation with a random policy: the critic's values converge to V(A) = {0}, V(B) = {1}, V(C) = {2} – the averages of what follows.
M8.ActorCritic.Explain.Actor: The actor now turns right at A {0}% of the time, right at B {1}%, left at C {2}%. Positive TD errors make the chosen move more likely, negative ones less likely – the policy drifts towards the largest reward.
M8.ActorCritic.Values.Tip: V(A), V(B), V(C) over runs. Dotted: exact values under the random policy (policy evaluation mode).
M8.ActorCritic.Policy.Tip: Probability of turning right in each state over runs.
M8.Bci.Title: Bidirectional brain–computer interfaces
M8.Bci.Lead: A brain–computer interface (BCI) turns neural signals into control commands. A classic one-way BCI records activity, extracts features and translates them into device commands. A bidirectional BCI adds a return path: it also delivers stimulation – to the brain, the spinal cord or the muscles – creating a true closed loop between nervous system and machine.
M8.Bci.C1.Title: Recording → processing → command
M8.Bci.C1.Text: Signal sources trade invasiveness against quality: EEG (scalp, non-invasive, low spatial resolution and SNR), ECoG (cortical surface, better signal, needs surgery), LFP (intracortical population signal) and single units (intracortical microelectrodes, most information but long-term stability problems). The pipeline: recording, A/D conversion, feature extraction, translation algorithm, device command.
M8.Bci.C2.Title: Artificial recurrent connection
M8.Bci.C2.Text: If a cortical cell's firing reliably accompanies an intended movement, the BCI can convert it into functional electrical stimulation (FES) of a paralysed muscle – bypassing a lesioned pathway. Two units can drive flexor and extensor separately. Unlike a robot arm, the subject's own muscles and sensory feedback stay in the loop. Stimulating the spinal cord instead can recruit existing spinal circuits and more natural muscle synergies.
M8.Bci.C3.Title: The Neurochip: autonomous closed loop
M8.Bci.C3.Text: A compact implantable or wearable device records neural and muscle signals, discriminates spikes, processes them on board, stores data and delivers programmable constant-current stimulation – with low latency, during natural behaviour, for days. The BCI is then not just a decoder but an adaptive intervention that can itself reshape neural connections.
M8.Bci.C4.Title: Inducing plasticity: timing is everything
M8.Bci.C4.Text: If each spike of a cortical neuron triggers stimulation near its target after a fixed delay, Hebbian/STDP mechanisms can strengthen the connection (Jackson, Mavoori & Fetz 2006): after a night of conditioning the same cortical spike produced a larger muscle response (post-spike facilitation). The effect depends on the spike–stimulus delay: strongest for short delays, absent for long ones – an STDP-like window. Clinically this suggests closed-loop rehabilitation after stroke or spinal cord injury, with challenges of electrode stability, safety, power, decoder drift, latency and ethics.
M8.Bci.Formulas:
source → transform → target | Design space: where we read, how we convert, where we stimulate.
I_stim = g · [r̂ − θ]⁺ | Rate-to-stimulation mapping: decoded rate above threshold sets the FES current.
Δw ∝ exp(−d / τ)   (d = spike → stimulus delay) | Conditioning window: short causal delays strengthen most.
PSF = STA(EMG)(t) after the spike | Connection strength read out as post-spike facilitation.
M8.Bci.Bio: Corticomotoneuronal cells project directly onto spinal motoneurons; their spike-triggered averages of EMG show post-spike facilitation. Moritz, Perlmutter & Fetz (2008) showed monkeys learning to control FES of temporarily paralysed wrist muscles with single cortical cells – even with cells not originally related to the movement.
M8.Bci.ML: Decoders range from direct thresholding and hand-tuned functions to Kalman filters and neural networks; adaptive (co-adaptive) decoders and reinforcement learning address non-stationarity of recordings and the brain's own learning.
M8.Bci.Takeaways:
A bidirectional BCI records, processes in real time and stimulates: a closed loop.
It can create an artificial connection that bypasses a lesion (cortex → FES → muscle).
Spike-triggered stimulation can induce Hebbian/STDP-like plasticity.
The spike–stimulus delay is critical: short causal delays strengthen, long ones hardly change.
M8.Bci.A1: It not only reads neural signals but also sends activity-dependent stimulation back into the nervous system or an effector.
M8.Bci.Q2: What is the difference between replacing a function and inducing plasticity with a BCI?
M8.Bci.A2: In the first case the BCI artificially bypasses a damaged pathway; in the second, timed stimulation tries to create a lasting biological strengthening of a connection.
M8.Bci.Q3: Why is the spike–stimulus delay critical in Hebbian conditioning?
M8.Bci.A3: Because plasticity is window-dependent: the order and delay of events determine the direction and size of the change.
M8.Bci.Q4: How can the strength of a corticomuscular connection be measured?
M8.Bci.A4: By the spike-triggered average of the muscle EMG: the post-spike facilitation peak after the cortical spike.
M8.Bci.Guide:
Watch the wrist follow the yellow target: the cortical units fire, the chip decodes their rates and stimulates the muscles.
Switch the BCI off: the natural pathway is lesioned, so the hand stops moving.
Turn off the automatic target and move the intention slider yourself.
Raise the threshold or lower the gain: the arm becomes weak and lags behind.
Below: set a 20 ms delay and run a night of conditioning; then try 80 ms and the random control – compare the facilitation.
M8.Bci.SimpleTitle: In plain words: an electronic bridge over a broken road
M8.Bci.Simple: After a spinal injury, the brain may still want to move the hand, but the “road” to the muscles is broken. A bidirectional BCI builds a bridge: it listens to a few brain cells, notices when they get busy, and sends small electric pulses directly to the muscles – the hand moves again. And if the bridge is used with the right timing, the brain's own weak connections can even grow stronger, a bit like a path that becomes wider the more people walk on it at the right moment.
M8.Bci.Fes.Tip: Two recorded cortical units drive functional electrical stimulation of a flexor and an extensor muscle.
M8.Bci.Enabled.Tip: Off: the natural pathway is lesioned and nothing reaches the muscles.
M8.Bci.AutoTarget.Tip: The subject tries to follow a slow sinusoidal target and modulates the cells accordingly.
M8.Bci.Intent.Tip: −1 = extend, +1 = flex. The flexor cell fires more for flexion, the extensor cell for extension.
M8.Bci.Gain.Tip: FES current per Hz of decoded rate above threshold.
M8.Bci.Threshold.Tip: Decoded rates below this produce no stimulation (avoids stimulating on background firing).
M8.Bci.FesReadout:
F {0} Hz · E {1} Hz   I_F {2} mA · I_E {3} mA
wrist {4}° · tracking error {5}°
M8.Bci.Fes.On: The loop is closed: cortical activity → decoded rate → stimulation → muscle force → movement.
M8.Bci.Fes.Off: BCI off: the cells still fire, but with the pathway lesioned no signal reaches the muscles.
M8.Bci.Loop.Tip: Left: two cortical units (F flexor, E extensor) flashing on spikes. Middle: the Neurochip with decoded rates and threshold (dashed). Right: the forearm; muscle brightness = stimulation; dashed yellow hand = target.
M8.Bci.Conditioning.Tip: Every spike of the recorded cortical cell triggers a stimulus near its spinal target after the chosen delay (Jackson et al. 2006).
M8.Bci.Delay.Tip: Time between the cortical spike and the triggered stimulus.
M8.Bci.Random.Tip: The same number of stimuli, but not locked to the spikes – no consistent causal order.
M8.Bci.Night.Tip: Simulates 10 hours of free behaviour with the Neurochip running (plays in about 3 s).
M8.Bci.CondReadout: conditioned {0} h   pairings {1} thousand   strength {2}% of baseline
M8.Bci.Cond.Short: Short causal delay: the stimulus arrives just after the spike – the STDP-like window gives strong potentiation.
M8.Bci.Cond.Long: Long delay: the stimulus comes too late to be paired with the spike – little change.
M8.Bci.Cond.Control: Random timing: potentiation and depression cancel on average – the connection does not strengthen.
M8.Bci.Sta.Tip: Spike-triggered average of the muscle EMG: grey before conditioning, green now. The bump ~10 ms after the spike measures the connection strength.
M8.Bci.Window.Tip: Line: the model's conditioning window. Dots: measured effects of your conditioning runs at different delays (scaled to the best one).
